metadata.title: PCR Using Q5® High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (NEB #M0491)
metadata.purpose: This protocol describes methods for PCR using Q5® High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase, which offers high fidelity (~280X higher than Taq), resulting in ultra-low error rates. Please note that protocols with Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase may differ from protocols with other polymerases. The conditions recommended below should be used for optimal performance.
metadata.scope: 25 µl or 50 µl routine PCR using Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (NEB #M0491) with 5X Q5 Reaction Buffer, dNTPs, primers, template DNA, and optional Q5 High GC Enhancer. Primer sequences, template identity, annealing temperature, and cycle count are assay-specific. Confirm the current manufacturer protocol and local laboratory policy before bench use.
beforeYouBegin: Use of high quality, purified DNA templates greatly enhances the success of PCR. Recommended amounts of DNA template for a 50 µl reaction are as follows: Genomic DNA 1 ng–1 µg; Plasmid or Viral 1 pg–10 ng.

Oligonucleotide primers are generally 20–40 nucleotides in length and ideally have a GC content of 40–60%. Computer programs such as Primer3 can be used to design or analyze primers. The best results are typically seen when using each primer at a final concentration of 0.5 µM in the reaction.

Use of the NEBTm Calculator is highly recommended to determine the annealing temperature when using this enzyme. Optimal annealing temperatures for Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase tend to be higher than for other PCR polymerases.

Mg++ concentration of 2.0 mM is optimal for most PCR products generated with Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase. When used at a final concentration of 1X, the Q5 Reaction Buffer provides the optimal Mg++ concentration.

The final concentration of dNTPs is typically 200 μM of each deoxynucleotide. Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase cannot incorporate dUTP and is not recommended for use with uracil-containing primers or templates. Should uracil-containing primers or templates be used, we recommend Q5U® Hot Start High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (NEB #M0515).

The 5X Q5 Reaction Buffer provided with the enzyme is recommended as the first-choice buffer for robust, high-fidelity amplification. The 5X Q5 Reaction Buffer is detergent-free and contains 2.0 mM Mg++ at the final (1X) concentration.

We generally recommend using Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase at a final concentration of 20 units/ml (1.0 unit/50 μl reaction). However, the optimal concentration of Q5 Hot Start High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase may vary from 10–60 units/ml (0.5–3 units/50 μl reaction) depending on amplicon length and difficulty.

Amplification of some difficult targets, like GC-rich sequences, may be improved by the addition of 1X Q5 High GC Enhancer. The Q5 High GC Enhancer is not a buffer and should not be used alone. It should be added only to reactions with the Q5 Reaction Buffer when other conditions have failed.

steps.action: Assemble all reaction components on ice. Each component should be gently mixed before adding to the reaction in a sterile thin-walled PCR tube.
steps.criticalNotes: Amplification of certain long, complex DNA targets (≥ 5 kb) may benefit from using a lower primer concentration (~ 0.2 to 0.3 µM).

steps.action: The Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase may be diluted in 1X Q5 Reaction Buffer just prior to use to reduce pipetting errors.
The entire reaction should be mixed again to ensure homogeneous, consistent mixture. Collect all liquid to the bottom of the tube with a quick centrifuge spin if necessary.
Overlay the sample with mineral oil if using a PCR machine without a heated lid.
Quickly transfer the reactions to a thermocycler preheated to the denaturation temperature (98°C) and begin thermocycling.

parameters.rawText: thermocycler preheated to the denaturation temperature (98°C)

steps.action: Perform thermocycling according to the Thermocycling Conditions for a Routine PCR (table t2). An initial denaturation of 30 seconds at 98°C is sufficient for most amplicons from pure DNA templates. Longer denaturation times can be used (up to 3 minutes) for templates that require it. During thermocycling, the denaturation step should be kept to a minimum. Typically, a 5–10 second denaturation at 98°C is recommended for most templates.

repeat.notes: 25–35 cycles. Generally, 25–35 cycles yield sufficient product. For genomic amplicons, 30-35 cycles are recommended.

parameters.rawText: Annealing 50–72°C 10–30 seconds. Use of the NEBTm Calculator is highly recommended.

steps.criticalNotes: Optimal annealing temperatures for Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase tend to be higher than for other PCR polymerases. The NEB Tm Calculator should be used to determine the annealing temperature when using this enzyme. A temperature gradient can also be used to optimize the annealing temperature for each primer pair. For high Tm primer pairs, two-step cycling without a separate annealing step can be used.

sourceReferences.location: Thermocycling Conditions table; Denaturation, Annealing, Cycle number sections

steps.action: Set extension time based on amplicon size and template type according to table t4. Extension times are generally 20–30 seconds per kb for complex, genomic samples, but can be reduced to 10 seconds per kb for simple templates (plasmid, E. coli, etc.) or complex templates < 1 kb. Extension time can be increased to 40 seconds per kb for cDNA or long, complex templates, if necessary. When amplifying products > 6 kb, it is often helpful to increase the extension time to 40–50 seconds/kb.

parameters.valueText: 20–30 seconds per kb for complex, genomic samples; 10 seconds per kb for simple templates; 40 seconds per kb for cDNA or long, complex templates
parameters.rawText: Extension times are generally 20–30 seconds per kb for complex, genomic samples, but can be reduced to 10 seconds per kb for simple templates (plasmid, E. coli, etc.) or complex templates < 1 kb. Extension time can be increased to 40 seconds per kb for cDNA or long, complex templates, if necessary.

steps.action: A final extension of 2 minutes at 72°C is recommended.

The PCR products generated using Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase have blunt ends. If cloning is the next step, then blunt-end cloning is recommended. If T/A-cloning is preferred, the DNA should be purified prior to A-addition, as Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase will degrade any overhangs generated. The Monarch® Spin PCR & DNA Cleanup Kit (5 μg) (NEB #T1130) is recommended as an efficient method for purification and concentration up to 5 μg of high-quality, double-stranded and single-stranded DNA.
steps.criticalNotes: If T/A-cloning is preferred, the DNA should be purified prior to A-addition, as Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase will degrade any overhangs generated. Addition of an untemplated -dA can be done with Taq DNA Polymerase (NEB #M0267) or Klenow exo– (NEB #M0212).

acceptanceCriteria.description: Expected single band at correct amplicon size on agarose gel.

steps.action: When primers with annealing temperatures ≥ 72°C are used, a 2-step thermocycling protocol (combining annealing and extension into one step) is possible.

controls.name: No-template control (NTC)
controls.description: Substitute nuclease-free water for template DNA. No amplification product should be visible.
controls.notes: The source protocol does not explicitly specify controls. A no-template control is standard practice for PCR and should be included to monitor for contamination.

controls.name: Positive-control template/primer pair
controls.description: Include a known template/primer pair that reliably amplifies under Q5 conditions to confirm reagent activity.
controls.notes: The source protocol does not explicitly specify a positive control. A positive control is recommended to verify that reagents and cycling conditions are functional.

expectedOutputs: Single band at the correct amplicon size on an agarose gel.
The PCR products generated using Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase have blunt ends.
No visible product in the no-template control.
Ultra-low error rate amplification due to Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase fidelity (~280X higher than Taq).

troubleshooting.problem: No PCR product or very low yield
troubleshooting.cause: Annealing temperature too high, insufficient template, primer design issues, or inhibitor carryover.
troubleshooting.solution: Use the NEB Tm Calculator to determine the correct annealing temperature. Increase template amount within recommended range (Genomic 1 ng–1 µg; Plasmid or Viral 1 pg–10 ng). A temperature gradient can also be used to optimize the annealing temperature for each primer pair.
troubleshooting.notes: Derived from General Guidelines; the source protocol does not include an explicit troubleshooting section.

troubleshooting.cause: Annealing temperature too low, excessive cycle number, or nonspecific primers.
troubleshooting.solution: Increase annealing temperature using the NEB Tm Calculator. Reduce cycle number (generally 25–35 cycles yield sufficient product). Redesign primers to be 20–40 nucleotides in length with a GC content of 40–60%.
troubleshooting.notes: Derived from General Guidelines; the source protocol does not include an explicit troubleshooting section.

troubleshooting.problem: Poor amplification of GC-rich or difficult templates
troubleshooting.cause: Secondary structure or high GC content in the template.
troubleshooting.solution: Amplification of some difficult targets, like GC-rich sequences, may be improved by the addition of 1X Q5 High GC Enhancer. The Q5 High GC Enhancer is not a buffer and should not be used alone. It should be added only to reactions with the Q5 Reaction Buffer when other conditions have failed.
troubleshooting.notes: Solution text is verbatim from the Mg++ and additives section of the source protocol.

troubleshooting.problem: Weak amplification of long or complex templates (> 6 kb)
troubleshooting.cause: Insufficient extension time for amplicon length.
troubleshooting.solution: When amplifying products > 6 kb, it is often helpful to increase the extension time to 40–50 seconds/kb. Extension time can be increased to 40 seconds per kb for cDNA or long, complex templates, if necessary.
troubleshooting.notes: Solution text is verbatim from the Extension and Amplification of long products sections of the source protocol.

troubleshooting.problem: Failed T/A cloning of Q5 PCR products
troubleshooting.cause: Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase generates blunt-end products and will degrade any overhangs generated.
troubleshooting.solution: If T/A-cloning is preferred, the DNA should be purified prior to A-addition, as Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase will degrade any overhangs generated. Addition of an untemplated -dA can be done with Taq DNA Polymerase (NEB #M0267) or Klenow exo– (NEB #M0212). If cloning is the next step, then blunt-end cloning is recommended.
troubleshooting.notes: Solution text is verbatim from the PCR product section of the source protocol.

safety.description: Wear appropriate personal protective equipment (lab coat, gloves, and eye protection) during all steps of the protocol. Use nuclease-free tubes and filtered tips for reaction setup.
safety.notes: The source protocol does not include an explicit safety section. Standard molecular biology laboratory safety practices apply.

safety.description: Ethidium bromide or other nucleic acid stains used for agarose gel analysis may be mutagenic or hazardous. Follow institutional safety guidelines for handling and disposal of gel staining reagents.
safety.notes: The source protocol does not include an explicit safety section. This note applies if agarose gel analysis is performed as a downstream QC step.

safety.description: UV transillumination used for gel visualization can cause skin and eye damage. Use appropriate UV shielding and eye protection.
safety.notes: The source protocol does not include an explicit safety section. This note applies if UV visualization is used for gel analysis.

limitations: The linked protocol does not select primer sequences, template identity, annealing temperature, or a fixed cycle count. These parameters are assay-specific and must be determined by the user. Amplification of certain long, complex DNA targets (≥ 5 kb) may benefit from using a lower primer concentration (~ 0.2 to 0.3 µM).
